context.title: About Unix Timestamp Converter
content: Unix Timestamp is the count of seconds that have elapsed since January 1, 1970 00:00:00 UTC. It is a standard for tracking time in computer systems and is widely used in operating systems, databases, and web development.

This tool provides two-way conversion for 10-digit (seconds) and 13-digit (milliseconds) Unix Timestamps, suitable for backend API integration and data verification. 10-digit is common in PHP/MySQL; 13-digit is common in JavaScript/Java.
AguBear Tools supports date detection and real-time conversion to various timezones, helping developers debug quickly.

faq.a: A Unix Timestamp is the total seconds elapsed since January 1, 1970 00:00:00 UTC. It is a timezone-independent way to represent time.
10-digit timestamps represent 'seconds', common in Linux systems and databases; 13-digit timestamps represent 'milliseconds', common in JavaScript and high-precision timing applications.

faq.q: How to convert timestamp to date?
faq.a: You can use this tool to automatically detect digits and convert based on your input. In JavaScript, you can use new Date(timestamp * 1000) to handle second-level timestamps.

context.title: About MD5 and SHA Hashing
content: A Hash Function is an algorithm that converts input data of any length into a fixed-length string. Common algorithms include MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, etc. They are widely used for password storage, file integrity verification, and digital signatures.

MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5) produces a 128-bit (16-byte) hash value, typically expressed as a 32-digit hexadecimal number. Although MD5 is no longer considered cryptographically secure, it is still commonly used for checksum verification.
This tool runs entirely in your browser. Your data is not sent to any server, ensuring privacy and security.

faq.a: No, MD5 is a 'hash', not encryption. Encryption is usually reversible (can be decrypted), whereas hashing is one-way and cannot be reversed to the original data.

faq.q: What is the difference between SHA-256 and MD5?
faq.a: SHA-256 is more secure and has a lower collision probability than MD5, producing a longer hash (64 characters vs 32 characters). Modern security applications recommend using SHA-256 or higher.
